Formatting rules

Put a formatting code before the characters you want to style. This guide explains the supported forms, which registered style each form selects, and how styles combine. It also shows how to measure and wrap formatted text without drawing it.

Calls used in the examples

Calls used in this guide
Call or settingArgumentsWhat it does
ChromaticText.compile(text)Formatted input stringParse the text into a reusable layout.
layout.width(characterWidth)Function measuring one characterMeasure visible glyphs using the same character widths as the renderer.
trim(width, reverse, characterWidth)Width limit; direction; measuring functionKeep text within a width while retaining formatting.
wrap(width, characterWidth)Line width; measuring functionInsert line breaks using the supplied widths.

When you finish: Compiled layouts are data values and need no close call. If your addon installs custom codes, retain the returned registration receipts and close them when unloading those codes. Font-based measuring and drawing belong on the client thread.

Code forms

A formatting token is one complete code, including its marker and any brackets or hex digits.

&z
A registered single-character color or effect. Character keys are converted to lowercase.
&[name]
Registered named color, effect or outline. Names are case-sensitive by default.
&x&F&F&C&C&0&0
A complete six-digit hex color in a 14-character token.
&[~wave:FF0000,0000FF]
An effect defined directly in the text: a wave with a red-to-blue palette.
§r or &r
Reset custom effects, colors, outlines and vanilla styles.

The section sign (§) can replace the ampersand (&) in these forms. Use the same marker before every digit in a complete hex token. Named triggers cannot contain control characters or square brackets.

Check which registered code a piece of text uses

A namespaced ID such as your_mod:gold identifies a registration; the trigger gold is what text uses as &[gold]. Triggers are shared across mods. Registering the same kind and exact trigger replaces its earlier entry, even when the IDs differ. Different kinds can keep entries for the same trigger.

The parser stops at the first match in these orders:

  • Ordinary character code: registered effect, then color, then outline.
  • Bracketed code: registered named effect, named color, enabled valid inline effect, then named outline. The outline step can split off a token-local color suffix.

Bracketed and hex forms are checked before ordinary character lookup. Choose a custom character such as z; x and [ introduce those syntax forms.

When named matching ignores case, Glow and glow remain separate registrations. Within each kind, the earlier spelling wins. Updating an exact spelling replaces its value without changing lookup order.

Inline definitions

An inline code defines an effect without registering a name first. It starts with &[~, ends with ], and must be enabled in the client settings. Between the tilde and closing bracket, use one of these forms:

  • colors for a stationary palette.
  • movement for an effect with its default palette and controls.
  • movement:colors to choose the effect and palette.
  • colorSpeed:moveSpeed:movement:colors to supply both effect controls.
  • animationSpeed:colorSpeed:moveSpeed:movement:colors to set playback speed separately.

A movement ID selects an effect type, such as wave or size. The effect reference lists the built-in IDs and explains their controls. Append semicolon-separated option=value settings to the movement, as in the last example:

&[~FF0000,0000FF]Static palette§r
&[~size]Large text§r
&[~0.5:1:1:wave;amplitudeY=2:FF0000,FFD000]Slow wave§r

Inline palettes and limits

A palette is a comma-separated list of colors. Inline palettes support three- or six-digit hex colors and the rainbow keyword. They are limited to 16 colors and 512 characters per definition. Parsed speed values clamp to -32 through 32. Inline extrusion permits at most 16 layers and explicit Matrix rows at most four per side; normal configuration/programmatic parameter limits permit up to 64 extrusion layers and 12 Matrix rows per side. Inline outline movements are excluded.

The inline API explains descriptor validation and the lifetime of saved effect identities.

Understand how codes combine and affect line width

  • Vanilla color codes (&0 through &f) and reset (&r) clear custom colors, effects, outlines and vanilla style flags.
  • Vanilla style codes k, l, m, n and o add obfuscation, bold, strikethrough, underline and italic respectively, keeping the active custom style.
  • A custom character, named or hex color changes the incoming color without removing an active effect. That effect may still choose its own output color.
  • A new primary effect replaces the earlier effect and clears its custom or vanilla color selection. It keeps the vanilla style flags and active outline. Another outline token replaces the previous outline.

Breathing, stretching, compression, spinning and shearing transform a whole run of text without changing the space it occupies in the line. Explicit size and letter spacing do change the width used to position following text.

An unrecognized ampersand marker is emitted as text, and parsing continues through the following characters. An unknown section-sign code consumes the marker and following character, selects white and clears the active styles. Width, trimming and wrapping preserve complete formatting tokens. Right-to-left ordering uses Minecraft's ICU text-shaping support.

Reverse trimming and wrapped continuations rebuild a formatting prefix. In that prefix, a custom color is emitted before the effect, which clears that color when reparsed. A custom color originally applied after an effect can therefore be lost, while the effect remains active. This can change the appearance of effects that use the incoming text color. Forward trimming keeps the original leading tokens and their order.

Reload text settings without losing the last valid values

Client settings are in config/chromatic_codes.cfg. Resource reload validates the complete configuration before applying any changes. Invalid input leaves the last valid settings active and preserves your file. These settings control the local appearance of text; they are not synchronized as server gameplay state.

A host such as GTWurtzitane may explicitly take over configuration through TextConfiguration.useExternalConfiguration(), then supply validated settings through the same application API. The standalone listener stops applying its own file.

Measure formatted text and fit it into a line

The example measures formatted text, wraps it into lines, and trims it to a chosen width. Supply a function returning each character’s ordinary width in your font. The example’s constant width of six only demonstrates the calls; Minecraft’s usual font gives different letters different widths.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.ChromaticText;
var layout = ChromaticText.compile("&[gold]ABC");
float width = layout.width(character -> 6);
String clipped = layout.trim(12, false, character -> 6);
String wrapped = layout.wrap(12, character -> 6);
var first = layout.glyphs().getFirst();
String visible = layout.plain();

val layout = ChromaticText.compile("&[gold]ABC")
val width = layout.width { 6 }
val clipped = layout.trim(12, false) { 6 }
val wrapped = layout.wrap(12) { 6 }
val first = layout.glyphs().first()
val visible = layout.plain()

def layout = text.compile('&[gold]ABC')
def width = layout.width({ c -> 6 } as java.util.function.ToIntFunction)
def clipped = layout.trim(12, false, { c -> 6 } as java.util.function.ToIntFunction)
def wrapped = layout.wrap(12, { c -> 6 } as java.util.function.ToIntFunction)
def first = layout.glyphs().getFirst()
def visible = layout.plain()

val layout = net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.ChromaticText.compile("&[gold]ABC")
val width = layout.width(_ => 6)
val clipped = layout.trim(12, false, _ => 6)
val wrapped = layout.wrap(12, _ => 6)
val first = layout.glyphs().getFirst()
val visible = layout.plain()

val layout = Text.compile("&[gold]ABC");
val width = layout.width(function(character) { return 6; });
val clipped = layout.trim(12, false, function(character) { return 6; });
val wrapped = layout.wrap(12, function(character) { return 6; });
val first = layout.glyph(0);
val rgb = layout.color(0);
val visible = layout.plain();

Glyphs retain complete visible Unicode text and raw UTF-16 start/end offsets. The width callback receives one UTF-16 code unit, matching the Java parser contract. Effects and bold flags affect measured advance. Continuation prefixes use the existing parser’s reconstruction rules; see the syntax guide for mixed color/effect limitations. Custom colors/outlines return -1 when absent in the ZenScript layout.

Choose how text refers to a color or effect

Choose a short character code such as &z, a readable name such as &[gold], or an effect object used directly by your code. The examples register each kind. Character and named colors, effects, and outlines are separate entry categories.

var color = ChromaticDefinitions.register(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.COLOR_CHAR,
    new ResourceLocation("my_mod", "gold_char"), 'Z', 0xFFCC00, null);
var direct = ChromaticDefinitions.register(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT,
    new ResourceLocation("my_mod", "direct_wave"), null, null, effect);
// Retain both receipts until unload.

val color = formattingCode(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.COLOR_CHAR,
    ResourceLocation("my_mod", "gold_char"), trigger = 'Z', rgb = 0xFFCC00)
val direct = formattingCode(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT,
    ResourceLocation("my_mod", "direct_wave"), effect = effect)

text.characterColor('my_pack:gold_char', 'Z', 0xFFCC00)
text.characterEffect('my_pack:wave_char', 'Y', effect)
text.characterOutline('my_pack:outline_char', 'X')
text.directEffect('my_pack:direct_wave', effect)

val codes = definitions("my_mod") { text =>
  text.code(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.COLOR_CHAR, "gold_char", Char.box('Z'), Int.box(0xFFCC00))
  text.code(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT, "direct_wave", null, callback = effect)
}

Text.characterColor("my_pack:gold_char", "Z", 0xFFCC00);
Text.characterEffect("my_pack:wave_char", "Y", effect);
Text.characterOutline("my_pack:outline_char", "X");
Text.directEffect("my_pack:direct_wave", effect);

The registry’s current case-sensitivity rules apply. Character inputs must contain exactly one UTF-16 character; do not use a surrogate-pair emoji as a character trigger. Kotlin/Scala callers can also use one atomic Java editor block for dependent changes.
